summaries.title: Long yields slip on record-weak housing and a pullback in oil, while the 2-year holds near 4.8%
summaries.regime_note: Long end eases on soft data; front end anchored by hike bets
summaries.takeaway: The 10-year yield dipped about 2 bp to 5.12% and the 30-year about 4 bp to 5.43%, helped by very weak housing reports and oil easing back from its morning highs. The 2-year barely moved and ended near 4.79%, because traders still expect the Fed to raise rates by December. The moves were small, and sources disagree on the 2-year's direction, so this was a quiet, mixed day rather than a clear turn.

cross.read: Stocks edged up to 7,712.57 as money rotated into healthcare, utilities and other defensive sectors; tech lagged on AI and debt worries.
Small companies, which borrow more and are more sensitive to interest rates, led the gains as long yields eased.
The blue-chip index rose about 530 points to 52,495.88.
A softer dollar fit with slightly lower long-term US yields.
Oil hit about $112 in the European morning, then fell back on a report of a Qatar-Pakistan proposal to settle the US-Iran standoff.
Stock-market fear gauge eased, a calm backdrop for bonds.

drivers.title: Housing data comes in very weak
drivers.what: Housing starts fell 5.2% in September to a 1.221 million annual pace, well below the 1.30 million expected. Pending home sales (contracts signed on existing homes) fell 7.3% to an index of 66.0, the lowest since the series began in 2001.
drivers.why: Mortgage rates follow long-term Treasury yields, and with the 10-year above 5% buyers and builders are pulling back. A weaker housing market points to slower growth, which tends to pull long-term yields down.
drivers.response: The 10-year ended about 2 bp lower at 5.12% and the 30-year about 4 bp lower at 5.43%, according to closing quotes from Investrade and Trading Economics.
drivers.signal: High rates are clearly biting in housing. NAR's chief economist said mortgage rates 'could be topping out', but the bond market needs broader signs of slowing before yields fall much further.

drivers.title: Oil eases from its highs on Iran diplomacy report
drivers.impact: Took some inflation pressure off long-term yields
drivers.what: Brent crude peaked at $111.99 a barrel in the European session, then pulled back after a report (Al Araby Al Jadeed) of a Qatar-Pakistan compromise proposal between the US and Iran. Brent closed at $108.79, down 0.7%.
drivers.why: Oil feeds directly into inflation. When oil falls, investors worry a little less that inflation will force the Fed to keep raising rates, which lets long-term yields drift lower.
drivers.response: Newsquawk noted that higher energy prices no longer appeared to weigh on Treasuries as the session went on; long-end yields finished lower.
drivers.signal: Iran's foreign ministry called the US response 'incomplete and insufficient', so the diplomacy is fragile. Oil near $110 still keeps a floor under yields.

drivers.title: Strong Japanese bond auction supports Treasuries early
drivers.impact: Early support for Treasury prices
drivers.what: An overnight 20-year Japanese government bond auction drew bids worth more than five times the amount on offer.
drivers.why: Strong demand for long-term bonds abroad eases fears that global investors are going on a 'buyers' strike' for long-dated debt, which helps Treasuries too.
drivers.response: Treasury futures were a few ticks firmer in the European morning, with the JGB auction cited as one reason.
drivers.signal: Wednesday's 20-year Treasury auction is the next test of whether demand for long-term US debt holds up at yields above 5%.

At the same time Iran's Revolutionary Guards warned ships against crossing the mined route through Hormuz, and Iran called the US response insufficient, keeping the oil risk premium in place.

geo.title: Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia
geo.text: Bloomberg reported the UK is set to fly missions to Saudi Arabia to help defend against Houthi attacks. There was no visible effect on Treasuries.

summaries.title: Treasuries give back part of last week's rally as AI stocks rebound and oil stays above $109
summaries.regime_note: Risk-on rebound lifts yields across the curve
summaries.takeaway: Yields rose about 5 bp across the curve, with the 10-year back at 5.14% and the 2-year near 4.76%, undoing roughly a third of last week's drop. The main push came from a rebound in AI and chip stocks, which reduced the demand for safe-haven bonds, while Houthi attack claims on Saudi oil sites kept inflation worries alive. The weakest homebuilder confidence reading since 2012 did little to hold yields down.

cross.read: Stocks rose to 7,690.73 alongside higher yields: money moved back into stocks and out of bonds, a risk-on move rather than a rates scare.
Chipmakers bounced after an eight-day losing streak, easing last week's AI-spending worries that had driven investors into Treasuries.
The blue-chip index swung between gains and losses and ended almost unchanged at 51,966.03.
A slightly firmer dollar matched the rise in US yields.
Oil swung between about $107 and $110 on Houthi attack claims and a US waiver on some Russian energy sanctions, ending little changed but still near its highest since May.

drivers.title: AI stocks rebound, bonds lose their safe-haven bid
drivers.what: Chip and AI stocks recovered after last week's selloff over how costly AI data centers will be to fund. Nvidia rose 1.4% and the Nasdaq gained 1.1%; a chip-stock gauge rose about 1.6%.
drivers.why: Last week nervous investors moved money from stocks into Treasuries, which pushed bond prices up and yields down. When stocks steady, some of that money flows back out of bonds, so yields rise.
drivers.response: The 10-year yield rose about 6 bp to 5.14% and the 2-year about 5 bp to 4.76%, according to Newsquawk's settlement wrap. That reverses part of last week's 14.6 bp fall in the 10-year.
drivers.signal: Last week's bond rally depended heavily on stock-market fear. If tech keeps recovering, yields may drift back toward this month's highs above 5.3%.

drivers.title: Houthi claims on Saudi oil sites keep inflation risk in focus
drivers.impact: Added to upward pressure on yields into the afternoon
drivers.what: Yemen's Houthis claimed new attacks on Saudi energy, airport and military targets, including an Aramco facility in Yanbu and the Shaybah oilfield. Saudi authorities did not immediately confirm the claims.
drivers.why: Higher oil prices feed into inflation, and with inflation already running hot, they make it more likely the Fed keeps rates high or raises them again. That pushes yields up.
drivers.response: Oil peaked around 1:45 PM ET and the 10-year hit its day high near 5.15% at about 1:10 PM ET. Treasury futures bounced off their lows as oil eased into the settlement; Brent ended down 0.3% at $109.55.
drivers.signal: Oil headlines are moving bonds through the inflation channel. As long as Brent stays near $110, it is hard for yields to fall far.

drivers.title: Homebuilder confidence falls to a 14-year low
drivers.impact: Little market reaction
drivers.what: The NAHB housing market index fell to 29 in October from 32, below the 31 expected and the lowest since June 2012. Builders' view of sales over the next six months dropped to 32 from 37.
drivers.why: Mortgage rates track long-term Treasury yields, so 10-year yields above 5% are squeezing home buyers. Weak housing would normally argue for lower yields because it points to a slowing economy.
drivers.response: Yields rose anyway: the stock rebound and oil outweighed the soft data.
drivers.signal: High rates are clearly hurting housing. That damage could matter more for the Fed if it starts to spread to the wider economy.

macro.note: CME FedWatch pricing showed about 4 bp of hikes for the October 27–28 meeting and about 26 bp by December, according to Newsquawk, meaning traders see a quarter-point hike by December as the likely path. The Fed is in its quiet period before the meeting, so no officials spoke.

macro.note: Only bill auctions today: the 3-month bill sold at 4.095% (2.77 times covered) and the 6-month at 4.220% (2.84 times covered). A $13 billion 20-year bond auction follows Wednesday.

macro.note: China's third-quarter GDP grew 4.5% from a year earlier, against 4.6% expected. Canada's September CPI rose 3.1% from a year earlier, slightly below the 3.2% expected.

geo.text: Cost-of-living protests turned violent over the weekend, and French government bond yields rose more than German ones on worries about higher state spending. The spillover to Treasuries was small.

geo.title: US waiver on Russian energy sanctions
geo.text: A waiver of some sanctions and tariffs on Russian energy exports raised the prospect of more fuel supply, which helped cap oil, though analysts said it was unclear how it would work or how long it would last.

summaries.as_of: 4:00 PM ET (market close quotes; Treasury's official curve for today not yet posted)
summaries.title: Treasuries catch their breath after their best week since February as tech stocks slide again
summaries.takeaway: After Thursday's big rally, Treasuries barely moved: the 10-year yield edged up about 1 bp to 5.10% while the 2-year slipped to about 4.73%. For the week the 10-year fell roughly 15 bp, its best week since mid-February, as a selloff in chip and AI stocks pulled money into bonds. Hotter import prices and rising oil kept inflation worries alive, so yields did not fall further.

cross.read: Stocks fell to 7,659.44 even though yields were steady, so this was a tech-specific scare rather than a rates scare.
Chipmakers led losses: the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell 3.8% with all 30 members lower, and the Nasdaq had its worst week since June.
Energy shares cushioned the blue-chip index as oil climbed.
Stock-market fear rose sharply, the kind of backdrop that usually keeps demand for Treasuries firm.
US crude settled near $99 a barrel and Brent near $110, its highest since May, adding to inflation worries.

drivers.title: AI and chip selloff keeps bonds in demand
drivers.impact: Held yields near the week's lows
drivers.what: Chip and AI-infrastructure stocks fell again on worries about debt-funded data-center spending and Chinese chip competition. CoreWeave fell about 12%, Micron about 5.6% and AMD about 6%; the Nasdaq dropped 2.1%.
drivers.why: When investors get nervous about stocks, they often shift money into Treasuries. That extra buying pushes bond prices up and yields down, or at least stops yields from rising.
drivers.response: The 10-year yield stayed close to Thursday's level of about 5.09% and settled at 5.097%, after falling 14.6 bp over the week according to Investrade. Market reports called it Treasuries' best week since mid-February.
drivers.signal: For now, worries about growth and AI spending are outweighing inflation fears in the bond market. A rebound in tech stocks would test whether this week's rally can last.

drivers.title: Import prices and factory output beat forecasts
drivers.impact: Kept yields from extending the rally
drivers.what: September import prices rose 1.1% against a 0.8% forecast and are up 8.1% from a year earlier, the biggest annual rise since 2022, led by a 4.8% jump in fuel. Industrial production rose 0.7% against a 0.4% forecast.
drivers.why: Higher prices for imported goods can flow through to what consumers pay, and stronger factory output suggests the economy is not cooling fast. Both argue for the Fed keeping rates high or raising them, which pushes yields up.
drivers.response: The data added to a week of hot inflation reports (CPI and PPI) but did not move bonds much on their own; the 10-year finished only about 1 bp higher.
drivers.signal: Inflation pressure is broadening from energy into goods prices. That keeps a further Fed hike on the table even as stocks wobble.

drivers.title: Warsh declines to signal the next move
drivers.impact: Little market reaction
drivers.what: Speaking with IMF chief Kristalina Georgieva in Bangkok, Fed Chair Kevin Warsh was asked about a hike at the October meeting and said, "I don't prejudge meetings." He told investors to watch the data rather than rely on guidance from the Fed.
drivers.why: The 2-year yield tracks expectations for the Fed's policy rate over the next two years, so hints from the Fed chair can move it quickly.
drivers.response: Treasury yields were largely stable after the remarks, which came Thursday night US time. Yahoo Finance reported CME FedWatch odds of a December hike at 74.3%, up from 50.2% a month earlier, with most traders expecting no change in October.
drivers.signal: Without guidance, each data release carries more weight. The market expects a hike by December rather than this month.

summaries.title: A global tech rout sends investors into Treasuries, overpowering a red-hot PPI
summaries.regime_note: Flight to safety; long end leads the rally
summaries.takeaway: Producer prices jumped far more than expected and retail sales beat forecasts, yet Treasuries rallied hard as a selloff in technology stocks spread from Asia. The 10-year yield fell about 10 bp to roughly 5.09%, its lowest since late September, while the 2-year dropped about 5 bp to 4.76%. Long-term yields fell more than short-term ones, so the curve flattened again.

cross.read: Stocks recovered from a weak open to close at 7,744.81, helped by the drop in yields even as chip and AI shares stayed under pressure.
The tech-heavy index opened down about 1.3% before clawing back to a small gain, closing at 26,713.03.
Rotation into consumer, health care and financial shares lifted the Dow to 52,177.81.
Oil rose after a larger-than-expected drop in US crude inventories; energy costs were the main force behind the jump in producer prices.

drivers.title: Global tech selloff drives a rush into bonds
drivers.impact: 10-year about −10 bp, 30-year about −10 bp
drivers.what: A selloff in technology and chip stocks that began on Wednesday spread through Asia overnight: South Korea's Kospi fell about 8% and Japan's Nikkei about 5%, with worries about the sustainability of AI spending at the centre. US markets opened lower, with the Nasdaq down 1.3% and the Russell 2000 down 1.9% shortly after 9:30 AM ET.
drivers.why: When investors pull money out of stocks they often park it in Treasuries, which pushes bond prices up and yields down. Long-term bonds tend to benefit most because they are the classic safe-haven asset.
drivers.response: Treasuries had already rallied in Asian trading, and yields kept falling through the day. Market reports described it as the biggest one-day drop in US yields since August 2025, and Reuters said longer-dated yields reached their lowest since September 23. By 3:19 PM ET the 10-year was near 5.085% and the 30-year near 5.426%.
drivers.signal: For now, fear about stocks is outweighing fear about inflation in the bond market. If the tech selloff fades, some of today's rally could reverse.

drivers.title: Hot producer prices and strong retail sales barely dent the rally
drivers.impact: Yields briefly pared declines after 8:30 AM ET, then resumed falling
drivers.what: Producer prices for final demand rose 1.3% in September, after 0.5% in August, and 6.3% from a year earlier, the biggest monthly gain in four and a half years. Energy prices jumped 10.8% on the month and gasoline 20.3%. Excluding food and energy, producer prices rose 0.7% against a 0.3% forecast. Retail sales rose 0.8% versus 0.3% expected, though much of that came from gasoline stations; the control group used to estimate GDP rose only 0.1%.
drivers.why: Rising costs for businesses can feed into consumer prices later, and strong spending argues against the economy cooling. Both normally push yields up, especially for short maturities tied to Fed policy.
drivers.response: Yields bounced briefly after the 8:30 AM ET releases, and CME FedWatch odds of a quarter-point hike this month rose to nearly 34% from about 29%. Both moves faded: hike odds slipped back to about 27% and yields resumed their slide.
drivers.signal: Much of the inflation heat is coming from energy, which investors seem to treat as a temporary shock rather than a reason for much higher long-term rates.

drivers.title: Fed officials signal patience on October
drivers.impact: Helped the 2-year fall despite the hot data
drivers.what: San Francisco Fed President Mary Daly said further rate hikes are more likely than not to be needed but that she sees no need to move at the October 27–28 meeting. Reuters reported that comments from officials including Michelle Bowman and Daly tempered the hike bets that had jumped after Wednesday's CPI.
drivers.why: The 2-year yield tracks where markets think the Fed's policy rate is heading over the next couple of years, so signs the Fed will wait pull it lower.
drivers.response: Traders priced roughly a 71–73% chance that rates stay unchanged this month but about a 91% chance of a hike by December, according to Reuters.
drivers.signal: The market expects one more hike, but later rather than sooner. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's comments in Bangkok are the next test of that view.

summaries.title: Hot CPI jolts Treasuries, then the long end rallies back as stocks slide
summaries.regime_note: CPI spike fades; long end ends lower, 2-year edges up
summaries.takeaway: September's consumer price report came in hotter than expected, briefly pushing the 10-year yield to about 5.33% and lifting the odds of a Fed rate hike this month. Treasuries then rallied through the afternoon as stocks fell, and the 10-year finished about 3 bp lower at 5.19%. The 2-year still ended slightly higher near 4.80%, so the curve flattened again.

cross.read: Stocks fell to 7,718.94 as technology shares dropped 3% on rising rate-hike bets. The slide coincided with the afternoon rally in long-term Treasuries.
The dollar rose to around 102.5 after peaking near 102.9 at about 11 AM ET, as the inflation data supported higher US short-term rates.
Gold fell to roughly $4,100 an ounce; higher odds of a Fed hike make non-yielding assets less attractive.
Stock-market volatility rose to 16.82, a sign of more nervous risk appetite after the inflation surprise.

drivers.title: Hotter-than-expected September CPI
drivers.impact: 2-year briefly hit about 4.95% before settling near 4.80%
drivers.what: Consumer prices rose 3.7% from a year earlier, above the 3.6% forecast and up from 3.4% in August. The monthly gain was 0.6%, as expected, with gasoline accounting for more than half of it. Core prices, which exclude food and energy, rose 0.3% on the month against a 0.2% forecast and 2.6% on the year against 2.5% expected. Shelter, airfares and used cars were among the upside drivers.
drivers.why: The Fed raised rates in September and has signalled one more hike this year. A firmer core reading strengthens the case for hiking sooner, and the 2-year yield is the maturity most sensitive to that.
drivers.response: Right after the 8:30 AM ET release the 2-year jumped to about 4.95%, its highest since late September, and the 10-year rose to about 5.33%. LSEG data showed the chance of a hike at the October 28 meeting rising to about 40% in the morning from 22% before the report.
drivers.signal: Markets now treat October as a live meeting rather than a likely pause, and bets on a December hike firmed.

drivers.title: Afternoon rally erases the long-end selloff
drivers.impact: 10-year about −3 bp, 30-year about −4 bp at the close
drivers.what: Treasuries recovered through the afternoon while stocks slid, with the S&P 500 down about 1% by midday and the Russell 2000 down 2.2% by 2:25 PM ET. Coverage of the reversal also pointed to recent Fed comments suggesting no rush to hike again, and after the close San Francisco Fed President Mary Daly told Reuters more hikes are likely needed but she sees no need to move in October.
drivers.why: When stocks sell off, investors often move money into Treasuries, pushing yields down. Signs that the Fed will be patient also reduce the risk that rates rise quickly, which helps longer-term bonds most.
drivers.response: By late afternoon October hike odds had eased to about 33% (LSEG). The 10-year fell to 5.19% and the 30-year to about 5.52%, while the 2-year held roughly 1 bp higher, flattening the 2s10s curve to about 39 bp. The 10-year breakeven inflation rate was about 2.35%.
drivers.signal: The market reads hot inflation as a reason for a slightly higher policy rate, not a reason to demand much more for holding long-term debt.

drivers.title: Beige Book flags spreading fuel costs
drivers.impact: Reinforced the inflation worry; no clear yield reaction
drivers.what: The Fed's Beige Book survey of its 12 districts said price growth was moderate in most districts and accelerating in four, adding that "higher oil prices permeated all District reports." Diesel costs passed on through fuel surcharges were a recurring theme, while labor conditions were described as "little changed" and consumer spending as mostly flat. Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee called the CPI report discouraging, pointing to sticky services inflation.
drivers.why: If energy costs spread into other prices, inflation could stay high even with a cooling economy, which is the Fed's main worry.
drivers.response: Yields kept falling through the afternoon despite the report, suggesting traders saw it as confirming what the CPI had already shown.
drivers.signal: Oil, tied to the Iran war, remains the biggest swing factor for inflation and for how long the Fed keeps tightening.

summaries.title: Long-term yields slip after the holiday as Fed officials keep a December hike in view
summaries.regime_note: Long end eases; the 2-year edges up
summaries.takeaway: Treasuries reopened after Monday's Columbus Day holiday with a quiet, mixed day. The 10-year yield ended about 2 bp lower at 5.22% and the 30-year about 3 bp lower near 5.57%, while the 2-year edged up to 4.80% as three Fed officials said another rate hike is likely before year-end. With September CPI due Wednesday morning, traders mostly waited.

cross.read: Stocks closed essentially flat at 7,805.45 as mixed big-bank earnings and a chip-stock selloff offset each other, so equities gave bonds little direction.
The dollar slipped to around 102.2 and fell against every major currency as traders positioned ahead of the CPI report.
Oil fell about 2% early on reports of easing Russian diesel supply concerns, then recovered to settle near $94.14 as Middle East shipping risks returned to focus.
Spot gold eased to roughly $4,160 an ounce, a calm reading for a market still on edge about inflation.

drivers.title: Fed officials keep a December hike on the table
drivers.impact: Held the 2-year near 4.80% while longer yields fell
drivers.what: Boston Fed President Susan Collins said "it will be appropriate to raise rates a bit further before the end of the year." New York Fed President John Williams told Bloomberg News one more hike may still be appropriate this year but he sees no need for more in 2027, adding that "the economy is not overheating." Governor Waller said the surge in long-term yields is restraining housing and auto demand.
drivers.why: The 2-year yield tracks where markets think the Fed's policy rate is headed. Officials talking about another hike keep it from falling, while Williams' signal that the hiking cycle is close to its end limits how high longer-term yields need to go.
drivers.response: The 2-year edged up about 1 bp to 4.80% while the 10-year and 30-year fell, flattening the curve. Investing.com's Fed rate monitor showed the chance of a hike at the October 28 meeting at 23%, up from 19.5% a day earlier, with about 87% odds of at least one hike by December.
drivers.signal: The market sees October as a likely pause and December as the probable next hike; Wednesday's CPI is the next test of that view.

drivers.title: Long end gives back some of its recent selloff
drivers.impact: 30-year about −3 bp, 10-year about −2 bp
drivers.what: Early in the day the 10-year fell to about 5.19%, roughly 5 bp below Friday's close, before recovering most of that drop. It still finished the day lower, and is about 6 bp below last Tuesday's level after hitting 24-year highs earlier this month. An FXStreet analysis noted record investor buying of long-term Treasuries at these yields, including the largest net position in 10-year futures held by asset managers in CFTC data going back to 2006.
drivers.why: Long-term yields reflect inflation worries and heavy government borrowing, but at levels above 5% many investors see value in locking in income, which caps the selloff for now.
drivers.response: The 30-year finished near 5.57% and the 5s30s curve narrowed about 2 bp to 56 bp.
drivers.signal: Steady demand from long-term buyers is keeping the long end in a range for now; a hot inflation print could quickly test it.

drivers.title: Oil and stocks offer no clear direction
drivers.impact: Small
drivers.what: Oil swung from an early drop of about 2% to a small gain at the settlement. Stocks were flat as JPMorgan missed earnings forecasts while Goldman Sachs beat, and chip stocks fell after a Chinese rival flagged progress on a new memory chip design.
drivers.why: Oil feeds into inflation and risk-off moves in stocks can push investors toward Treasuries, but neither moved far enough on Tuesday to drive yields.
drivers.response: The early dip in oil coincided with the 10-year's low near 5.19%; as oil recovered, yields drifted back up.
drivers.signal: With oil still above $90, energy remains a source of inflation risk that bond investors are watching closely.

macro.note: Sales rose slightly from August and came in close to forecasts, so the report did little to move yields.

macro.title: Fed pricing
macro.note: Investing.com's Fed rate monitor (5:25 PM ET): 23% chance of a hike on Oct 28, up from 19.5% the prior day; about 87% chance of at least one hike by the Dec 9 meeting, up from about 84%. The policy rate is 3.75–4.00% after September's hike.

macro.title: Treasury supply
macro.note: No coupon auctions on Tuesday. Treasury's next quarterly borrowing announcement is due November 4.

Attacks on commercial ships near the Strait of Hormuz and Saudi-led strikes on a Houthi-linked oil facility in Yemen were also reported. These kept oil supported but had no clear effect on Treasuries.

summaries.title: Short-term yields edge up as consumers' inflation worries climb; long end holds steady
summaries.regime_note: Front end rises; the 30-year is little changed
summaries.takeaway: After Thursday's big swings, Treasuries had a quieter Friday ahead of a three-day weekend. The 2-year yield rose about 4 bp to 4.79% as a University of Michigan survey showed Americans expecting higher inflation and markets kept leaning toward another Fed hike later this year. The 10-year edged up about 1 bp to 5.24% and the 30-year was flat at 5.60%, so the curve flattened; the 10-year still ended the week about 5 bp lower, according to Trading Economics.

cross.read: Stocks rebounded to 7,811.54 as tech recovered from Thursday's selloff, leaving all three major indexes higher for the week. The rally took away some of the safe-haven demand that helped bonds on Thursday.
Brent settled near $104.72, little changed after dipping early on Trump's pledge not to attack Iran before the midterms; hurricane-related shutdowns of Gulf of Mexico oil output limited the decline.
December gold settled at $4,216.30 an ounce, up about $59, as inflation and geopolitical worries kept demand firm.
The stock market's fear gauge eased to 14.84, consistent with a calmer day across markets.

drivers.title: Consumers expect more inflation
drivers.impact: Added upward pressure on short-term yields
drivers.what: The University of Michigan's preliminary October survey showed sentiment falling to 46.3, below the 47.8 expected and September's 48.1. One-year inflation expectations rose to 4.7% from 4.6%, and five-year expectations rose to 3.5% from 3.4%. Survey director Joanne Hsu said "Frustration over cost-of-living continues to mount."
drivers.why: The Fed watches inflation expectations closely: if people expect prices to keep rising, inflation can become harder to bring down, which argues for higher rates for longer.
drivers.response: The 2-year yield, the one most tied to Fed expectations, ended about 4 bp higher at 4.79%, the biggest move on the curve. Weak sentiment on its own would normally pull yields down, so the inflation details appear to have mattered more.
drivers.signal: Rising long-term inflation expectations keep pressure on the Fed to hike again; that makes next Wednesday's CPI report especially important.

drivers.title: Fed hike expectations stay in place
drivers.impact: Kept the front end anchored at high levels
drivers.what: Trading Economics reported markets pricing roughly an 81–82% chance the Fed holds rates at its October 28 meeting, with a December hike still seen as likely. This follows comments this week from Governor Waller and St. Louis Fed President Musalem that more hikes will probably be needed.
drivers.why: When markets expect the Fed to raise rates again, short-term yields stay high and tend to rise on any sign of stubborn inflation.
drivers.response: With no major Fed news on Friday, the 2-year drifted higher alongside the inflation-expectations data, and the 2s10s curve flattened about 2 bp to 45 bp.
drivers.signal: The October meeting looks like a likely pause, but the market still expects the Fed's next move to be a hike rather than a cut.

drivers.title: Long end steadies after this week's auctions
drivers.impact: 30-year little changed (about −1 bp)
drivers.what: The 30-year yield finished near 5.60%, essentially where it closed Thursday after pulling back from its highest level since the early 2000s. Strong demand at this week's 10-year and 30-year auctions suggested investors are still willing to buy long-term debt at these yields. Investrade also reported a weekly record $19.78 billion flowing into bond funds.
drivers.why: Long-term yields had been climbing on worries about heavy government borrowing and inflation; solid buying interest eases those concerns, at least for now.
drivers.response: The long end held steady while short-term yields rose, which is why the curve flattened.
drivers.signal: If long-end demand stays healthy, the 30-year may settle into a range; a hot CPI could quickly test that.

drivers.title: Oil steady despite Iran pledge and Gulf hurricane
drivers.impact: Small; oil ended little changed
drivers.what: Oil slipped early after President Trump's pledge not to attack Iran before the November 3 midterms, but Hurricane Isaias shut in about 63% of Gulf of Mexico oil output, per TheStreet's report of the agency figure. Brent settled up about 0.4% near $104.72.
drivers.why: Oil prices feed directly into inflation, so they matter for how high the Fed may need to push rates.
drivers.response: With oil roughly flat, energy was not a major driver of yields on Friday, unlike Thursday's morning spike.
drivers.signal: Oil above $100 keeps inflation risk elevated; any escalation around Iran or the Strait of Hormuz could quickly push yields back up.

Short-term yields rose a few basis points while the 30-year stayed put, a pattern that points to Fed and inflation expectations rather than worries about long-term debt supply. The Michigan survey's rise in inflation expectations fits that story, but the moves were small, there was no major data release beyond the survey, and inflation-adjusted yields were not available to confirm the split, so conviction is low. Over the week, long-term yields hit 24-year highs and then pulled back after strong auctions.
interpretation.change: A hot September CPI on October 14 would likely push the 2-year higher and revive the long-end selloff; a soft reading could ease December hike bets.

summaries.title: Long yields reverse from 24-year highs after a solid 30-year auction
summaries.regime_note: Long end leads a turnaround; front end barely moves
summaries.takeaway: An oil spike on Iran reports pushed the 10-year yield to about 5.35% in the morning, its highest in 24 years, before yields turned around and finished at the day's lows. A solid $22 billion 30-year auction, President Trump's post that the US won't attack Iran before the midterms, and a tech-stock selloff all helped. By the close the 10-year was about 5 bp lower at 5.23% and the 30-year about 6 bp lower at 5.60%, while the 2-year slipped only about 1 bp as Fed officials kept talking about more hikes.

cross.read: Stocks fell to 7,765.36 and the Nasdaq dropped 1.25% after a report that OpenAI's revenue is lower than thought hit chipmakers; some of that money moved into bonds late in the day.
Brent rose to about $104 on reports of possible US strikes on Iran, but came off its highs after Trump said there would be no attack before the midterms.
The Bloomberg dollar index was little changed; the dollar firmed in Europe, then lagged in US trading.
Gold edged up to about $4,156 an ounce as oil and geopolitical worries offered some support.

drivers.title: Solid 30-year auction
drivers.impact: Helped long yields fall from 24-year highs
drivers.what: Treasury sold $22 billion of 30-year bonds at 5.618%, essentially at the 5.617% yield traded just before the 1:00 PM ET sale (a tiny 0.1 bp "tail"). Bid-to-cover was 2.54 vs a 2.41 average, indirect bidders, a group that includes foreign buyers, took 72.3% vs a 69.1% average, and dealers were left with 6.8% vs a 10.3% average.
drivers.why: With the 30-year near its highest yield since the early 2000s, investors were watching for signs that buyers were tiring of long-term US debt. Strong outside demand, following Wednesday's well-received 10-year sale, eased that worry.
drivers.response: Treasuries rallied after the result and into the close; the 30-year ended about 6 bp lower at 5.60% after hitting a fresh 24-year peak earlier in the day.
drivers.signal: Two solid long-end auctions in a row suggest buyers are willing to step in at these yield levels, which may slow the long-end selloff for now.

drivers.title: Oil spike, then Trump's Iran comments
drivers.impact: Pushed yields up in the morning, eased the pressure in the afternoon
drivers.what: Oil jumped on reports that the US was considering strikes on Iran, with Brent topping $104 and the 10-year hitting about 5.35% in the morning. Around 1:00 PM ET, oil pared gains after Trump posted that the US would not attack Iran before the November 3 midterm elections.
drivers.why: Higher oil raises inflation risks, which can push the Fed to hike more and makes investors demand higher yields. A lower near-term risk of conflict trims that inflation fear.
drivers.response: Oil still closed sharply higher (Brent about +4%), but yields reversed from their morning highs and finished at the day's lows.
drivers.signal: Energy remains the main inflation wildcard for bonds; headlines about Iran and the Strait of Hormuz can move yields quickly in either direction.

drivers.title: AI stock selloff
drivers.impact: Added late support for Treasuries
drivers.what: A Financial Times report put OpenAI's annualized revenue at about $50 billion, roughly $20 billion below earlier reports. Chip stocks fell sharply in the afternoon, with Nvidia −2.9%, AMD −3.9% and Micron −4.8%.
drivers.why: When stocks fall, some investors move money into safer government bonds, and doubts about AI spending can also weigh on growth expectations.
drivers.response: The Nasdaq fell 1.25% and the S&P 500 0.47%, while the 10-year closed at its low of the day.
drivers.signal: If doubts about the AI boom spread, bonds could get more support from investors seeking safety, even with inflation still high.

drivers.title: Fed officials keep hikes on the table
drivers.impact: Kept the 2-year steady (−1 bp)
drivers.what: Governor Christopher Waller said "I anticipate additional hikes to support a timelier return of inflation to our 2% goal," adding that "the hikes do not need to come at consecutive meetings." St. Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem signaled rate increases over the next six to nine months but did not endorse a move at this month's meeting.
drivers.why: The 2-year yield tracks expected Fed policy. Officials talking about more hikes, but with flexible timing, fits the market's view of a hold in October and a likely hike later.
drivers.response: The 2-year ended only about 1 bp lower at 4.75%, far less than the long end, so the curve flattened. Trading Economics reported markets pricing roughly a 78% chance of an October hold and about a 69% chance of a December hike.
drivers.signal: The front end is anchored by Fed hike expectations; next week's September CPI is the next big test of those expectations.

In the afternoon, a solid 30-year auction, a calmer tone on Iran and a stock selloff turned yields lower, and they closed at the day's lows. drivers.title: Strong 10-year auction
drivers.impact: Pulled the 10Y back from its 2002-era highs
drivers.what: Treasury sold $39 billion of 10-year notes at 5.300%, below the 5.317% yield traded just before the sale (a 1.7 bp "stop-through"). Bid-to-cover was 2.77 vs a 2.54 average, and indirect bidders, a group that includes foreign buyers, took 80.3% vs a 74.1% average. Dealers were left with just 2.5%.
drivers.why: With yields at multi-decade highs and heavy government borrowing, investors were worried buyers might demand even higher yields. A sale that clears below the pre-auction yield with strong outside demand eases that fear.
drivers.response: Yields eased from the day's highs after the 1:00 PM ET result, leaving the 10-year only about 2 bp higher on the day.
drivers.signal: Demand for long-term US debt is still there at these yield levels, which may slow the long-end selloff. Thursday's 30-year sale is the next test.

drivers.title: Fed minutes keep a year-end hike in play

drivers.signal: Markets read the minutes as "wait in October, maybe hike in December," leaving upcoming inflation data as the deciding factor.

summaries.title: Yields ease back from 24-year highs as Fed hike bets fade
summaries.regime_note: Front end leads a modest pullback
summaries.takeaway: Treasury yields slipped after Monday's 24-year highs: the 2-year fell about 4 bp to 4.79% and the 10-year about 4 bp to 5.28%, while the 30-year dipped only 2 bp. The front end led as the market's odds of an October Fed hike sank to about 22%, and a dip in oil helped. The moves were small and the long end barely budged, so this looks like a pause in the selloff rather than a turn.

cross.read: Stocks closed at a record (7,818.93) as yields eased: lower borrowing costs and tech strength helped equities.
Gold rose to about $4,186 an ounce as yields and Fed hike odds came down.

drivers.title: Fed hike bets keep fading
drivers.what: CME FedWatch put the chance of a rate hike at the October 27–28 meeting at about 21.6%, down from roughly 51% a week earlier.
drivers.why: Friday's weak September jobs report (just 29,000 payrolls added) made another hike after September's look less necessary. The 2-year yield is the maturity most tied to where the Fed sets rates, so it moves most when hike odds change.
drivers.response: The 2-year fell about 4 bp and the 10-year about 4 bp, while the 30-year eased only 2 bp, so the 2s10s curve steepened slightly to about 48 bp.
drivers.signal: A front-end-led rally says traders are trimming the odds of more Fed tightening, not that worries about long-term borrowing have gone away.

drivers.title: Oil dips on improving Gulf supply
drivers.impact: Took some pressure off yields
drivers.what: Brent crude fell as low as $97.8 a barrel during the session before recovering toward $100. Saudi Arabia restored its East-West pipeline to 5.8 million barrels a day and G7 countries have been releasing emergency reserves.
drivers.why: Oil near $100 has been a big part of the inflation worry that pushed yields to multi-decade highs. Any sign of steadier supply eases that worry a little.
drivers.response: Yields drifted lower alongside oil, but the move was modest and oil itself ended well off its lows.
drivers.signal: Energy remains a two-way risk: oil relief helps bonds, but renewed attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz could quickly reverse it.

drivers.title: 3-year auction meets ordinary demand
drivers.impact: No directional read
drivers.what: Treasury sold $58 billion of 3-year notes at 4.932%, slightly below the yield expected just before the sale (stopped through by 0.3 bp). The bid-to-cover ratio was 2.62 vs a 2.65 average; foreign and other indirect buyers took 57.6% vs a 65.9% average.
drivers.why: This week's auctions test whether investors will absorb heavy government borrowing at yields near 24-year highs.
drivers.response: The sale passed without disruption, and yields stayed lower into the close.
drivers.signal: Adequate but not strong demand. The bigger tests are Wednesday's 10-year and Thursday's 30-year sales, where the long-end selloff has been concentrated.

macro.title: Trade deficit (August)
macro.note: Imports rose $17.2bn to $420.8bn and exports $4.5bn to $315.2bn. Little visible effect on Treasuries.

macro.title: 3-year note auction
macro.note: $58bn; stopped through by 0.3 bp; bid-to-cover 2.62 vs 2.65 average.

macro.title: Fed pricing
macro.note: CME FedWatch showed about a 21.6% chance of a hike on October 28 and 78.4% for a hold, after the September hike to 3.75%–4.00%. Vice Chair for Supervision Bowman spoke on bank regulation and did not discuss monetary policy.

geo.title: Strait of Hormuz shipping
geo.text: Oil flows have been recovering, which helped Brent dip below $98 intraday, but reports of stepped-up Iranian attacks on tankers kept prices near $100. This remains the main inflation risk hanging over bonds.

events.react: 2Y ends near 4.79% (−4 bp), 10Y near 5.28% (−4 bp), 30Y near 5.65% (−2 bp)

interpretation.text: The day's evidence points mildly toward easing Fed expectations: the 2-year led, hike odds kept falling, and the long end lagged. But the moves were only a few basis points after a large multi-week selloff, oil ended well off its lows, and inflation-adjusted yields were not available to confirm the split. Conviction is low: this reads as a pause, not a reversal.
interpretation.change: Weak demand at Wednesday's 10-year or Thursday's 30-year auction, or a hawkish tone in Wednesday's FOMC minutes, would likely send long yields back toward their highs; a soft CPI on October 14 would support today's direction.

summaries.title: Long-end yields grind to fresh 24-year highs as the curve keeps steepening
summaries.takeaway: The 10-year and 30-year yields rose 3 bp to 5.31% and 5.66%, the highest since 2002, while the 2-year barely moved. The whole 10-year move came from real yields, with inflation breakevens unchanged, so investors are asking for more pay to lend long rather than betting on a more hawkish Fed. A soft ISM services headline with hot prices did little to change that.

cross.read: Stocks rose and the Nasdaq hit a record despite higher long yields: tech strength outweighed bond weakness.
Oil stayed above $100 ($102.90), but breakevens did not move, so energy was not today's rates story.
US crude slipped to about $90.68; a mixed oil tape with no clear inflation signal.

drivers.title: Long end extends its selloff
drivers.what: The 10-year rose to 5.31% and the 30-year to 5.66% at Treasury's close, both up 3 bp and at their highest since 2002. The 2-year rose just 1 bp to 4.84%.
drivers.why: Long-dated government bonds are selling off around the world. France's 10-year yield is near 5% and its gap over Germany is close to 1.5 percentage points after a new budget met doubts from its fiscal watchdog. When investors worry about government borrowing, they want extra yield to hold long bonds.
drivers.response: 2s10s steepened 2 bp to 47 bp and 5s30s 3 bp to 60 bp. The 10-year real (TIPS) yield rose 3 bp to 2.95%; the 10-year breakeven was unchanged at 2.36%.
drivers.signal: Long-end and real-yield led, with the front end flat: a term-premium story, not a repricing of Fed policy or of inflation expectations.

drivers.title: ISM services: softer activity, hotter prices
drivers.impact: Mixed data; the prices index stood out
drivers.what: The ISM services PMI was 54.9 vs 55.0 expected and 55.4 in August. Business activity fell to 56.5 from 61.7, but the prices index rose to 74.0 from 72.6, its highest since July 2022, and employment rose back above 50 to 50.1.
drivers.why: Slower activity would normally pull yields down, but rising input costs keep inflation risk alive at a time when the Fed has been raising rates.
drivers.response: The 10-year still finished 3 bp higher on the day, and breakevens were unchanged, so the hot prices index did not show up as higher inflation expectations.
drivers.signal: The data did not give the market a reason to buy bonds: a slight growth miss was offset by price pressure.

drivers.title: Weak jobs report keeps a lid on the front end
drivers.impact: 2Y +1 bp; October hike odds stay low
drivers.what: Friday's September jobs report showed payrolls up just 29,000, unemployment at 4.2%, and the prior two months revised down by a combined 60,000.
drivers.why: A cooling job market makes another Fed hike at the October 27–28 meeting less likely, which anchors 2-year yields, the maturity most tied to Fed policy.
drivers.response: CME FedWatch put October hike odds near 24% on Monday. The 2-year is 8 bp lower than a week ago.
drivers.signal: With the Fed priced as likely to hold, the long end is doing the moving, which is why the curve steepened 15 bp (2s10s) over the week.

geo.title: France's budget and political risk
geo.text: France's 2027 budget targets a 5% deficit, but its fiscal watchdog questioned the growth assumptions. French 10-year yields near 5% are part of the global long-end selloff weighing on Treasuries.

geo.title: Middle East supply risk in oil
geo.text: Brent held above $100, but 10-year breakevens were unchanged, so oil added little to today's move in Treasuries.

events.react: No rally in bonds; the 10-year ended the day 3 bp higher

events.title: Stocks close higher; Nasdaq sets a record

interpretation.text: The evidence points to rising term premium: the long end rose while the 2-year was flat, real yields did all of the 10-year move, and breakevens did not budge. Fed expectations, if anything, eased after Friday's weak jobs data. Conviction is medium because the day's move was small and no single headline drove it; it is a continuation of a global long-bond selloff rather than a new shock.
interpretation.change: Weak demand at this week's 10-year or 30-year auctions would likely push long yields higher still; strong auctions, or a soft CPI on October 14, could halt the steepening.
